summary: For learners aged 10–11, build a model of matter cycling in ecosystems that traces a single parcel of nutrients around a closed loop (soil → plant → animal → dead matter → decomposers → soil) and contrasts the recycling of matter with the one-way flow of energy with heat transferred out of the ecosystem. The pivotal ideas: matter is recycled and never used up, while energy flows one way and is transferred out as dispersed heat, not destroyed; and decomposers (fungi, bacteria, worms) are the loop-closing node without which the cycle cannot complete. Learners describe the decomposer's role, trace matter through the full loop, and interpret or create a cycle diagram. This KS2/5-LS2-1 model is the foundation that KS3's carbon and water cycles later specialise.
misconceptions: Thinking matter is 'used up' and gone, rather than recycled endlessly through the ecosystem.
Omitting decomposers, so the cycle appears not to close and dead matter just vanishes.
Conflating matter cycling with energy flow — believing energy also cycles back, or that matter is lost like energy.
Assuming plants get their mass/matter mainly from the soil rather than understanding nutrient uptake as one part of a wider cycle.

activities.title: Drive a nutrient parcel around the matter cycle
steps: Follow a single labelled 'parcel' of nutrients as it moves out of the soil, into a growing plant's roots, into an animal that eats the plant, into the animal's dead remains, then into the decomposers (fungi, bacteria, worms) that break it down and hand the nutrients back to the soil — where the same parcel is taken up by the next plant.
At each step, state what matter is moving and which process moves it.

Turn the decomposers OFF and describe what happens: dead leaves and bodies pile up, nutrients stay locked in dead matter, the soil's available nutrients deplete, and new growth stalls because the loop no longer closes.
Explain in your own words why decomposers are the step that CLOSES the loop and why matter is recycled rather than consumed.
Watch a parallel one-way energy stream — sunlight entering and heat leaking away, never returning — and state the contrast: matter cycles, energy flows.
activities.insight: A cycle is a literal closed loop: the same matter returns to the beginning and is used again. Decomposers are the load-bearing step that closes the loop; without them nutrients lock up in dead matter. Matter is recycled endlessly, whereas energy flows one way and is transferred out of the ecosystem as dispersed heat, not destroyed.

activities.title: Read and build a closed-loop cycle diagram
steps: Study a labelled cycle diagram of soil → plant → animal → dead matter → decomposer → soil, and for each node and arrow state the process happening and what matter is moving.
Pay particular attention to the decomposer node — describe how fungi, bacteria and worms on a rotting log return nutrients to the soil.
Then construct your own cycle diagram from scratch, ensuring the end arrow feeds back into the beginning so the loop is genuinely closed.
Mark where new plant growth draws on the returned nutrients.
activities.insight: A canonical closed-loop diagram is the shared representation for matter cycling; being able to both read and produce one, with decomposers included, shows the loop actually closes.

activities.title: 'What if nothing ever rotted?' discussion and thought experiment
steps: Discuss or write a response to: 'What would happen to a forest if there were NO decomposers?'
Talk through how a decomposer differs from an ordinary animal that just eats.
Reason aloud about whether the same nutrient can be used more than once in an ecosystem, and explain how.
Trace one nutrient from a dead tree into a living plant to show matter is not destroyed when things rot.
activities.insight: Reasoning about a no-decomposer ecosystem reveals the decomposer's loop-closing role by exposing what breaks without it, and reinforces that matter is conserved and recycled.

activities.title: Check and discriminate the model
steps: Sequence the stages of the matter loop in order.
Answer targeted questions such as 'What returns nutrients to the soil?' and sort processes by what they do.
Decide which quantity is recycled and which is lost (matter cycles vs energy flows), and justify the choice.

Respond to this prompt: 'A fallen tree rots away on the forest floor until you can barely see it. Where has all its material gone — is it destroyed? Explain what the decomposers did with it, and how that material can end up in a new plant.'
activities.insight: Confirms the learner can trace the full loop including decomposers, conserves matter, and keeps matter cycling distinct from energy flow. These checks verify the model; they do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing the loop or explaining the decomposer role in their own words.

activities.title: Decomposition up close (optional tangible extension)
steps: Examine decomposers at work — for example fungi, bacteria and worms on a rotting log, or a short look 'under the soil' at a decomposing layer.
Connect what you observe to the cycle: name what the decomposers are breaking down and what they return to the soil.
Relate this general matter loop forward to the carbon and water cycles you will meet later, which are specific versions of the same idea.
activities.insight: Seeing real decomposition can make the abstract node tangible and links the systems loop to concrete organisms and to later carbon/water cycle study.

checkQuestion: Say: 'A fallen tree rots away on the forest floor until you can barely see it. Where has all its material gone — is it destroyed? Explain what the decomposers did with it, and how that material can end up in a new plant.'
checkAnswer: The material is NOT destroyed. Decomposers (fungi, bacteria, worms) break the dead tree down, returning its nutrients to the soil (and some carbon to the air). Those soil nutrients are taken up by new plants' roots and passed on to animals that eat the plants — so the matter cycles round again. Nothing is lost; it is recycled through the ecosystem.
